title: Linked List Cycle
statement: Given the head of a linked list, return `True` if the list contains a **cycle** — that is, if following `next` pointers eventually leads back to a node already visited.

example.input: head = [3,2,0,-4], where the last node links back to the node at index 1
example.why: After −4 the list goes back to 2, so walking it never ends.

idea: We could remember every visited node in a set and stop when one repeats, but that costs O(n) memory.
Instead, send two runners down the list: `slow` moves one node per step, `fast` moves two.
With no cycle, `fast` simply reaches the end. With a cycle, `fast` can never leave it and closes the gap to `slow` by one node per step — so they are guaranteed to meet.

complexity.timeWhy: Once both runners are in the cycle, the gap shrinks by one every step.

steps.text: Our example input is drawn on the stage. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Two runners: `slow` takes 1 step at a time and `fast` takes 2. If there is a loop, `fast` cannot run off the end — it keeps circling and must catch `slow`.
`slow` steps to node 2; `fast` jumps two nodes to node -4.
`slow` steps to node 0; `fast` jumps two nodes to node 0.
`slow` and `fast` are standing on the **same node** (0). That can only happen inside a loop.
The runners met, so the list has a cycle → **True**.
Done — the answer is **`True`**. After −4 the list goes back to 2, so walking it never ends.
